content: When changing antiretroviral (ARV) regimens in individuals experiencing virologic failure with HIV RNA levels greater than 1,000 copies/mL, drug-resistance testing is strongly recommended (AI). For those with HIV RNA levels between 500 and 1,000 copies/mL, resistance testing may be less successful but should still be considered (BII). Drug-resistance testing should also be performed in cases of suboptimal viral load reduction (AII). In individuals failing integrase strand transfer inhibitor (INSTI)-based regimens, genotypic testing for INSTI resistance is necessary to determine whether an INSTI drug should be included in subsequent regimens (AII). Resistance testing in the context of virologic failure should ideally be conducted while the patient is still taking the prescribed ARV drugs or, if not feasible, within four weeks of discontinuing therapy (AII). If more than four weeks have passed since ARV discontinuation, resistance testing may still provide useful information, though previously selected resistance mutations may not be detected (CIII). Genotypic resistance testing is the preferred method for guiding therapy in patients with suboptimal virologic responses or virologic failure while on their first or second ARV regimens (AII). For individuals with known or suspected complex drug-resistance mutation patterns, particularly to protease inhibitors (PIs), adding phenotypic testing to genotypic testing is generally preferred (BIII). Genotypic resistance testing is recommended for all pregnant women before initiating antiretroviral therapy (ART) (AIII) and for those entering pregnancy with detectable HIV RNA levels while on therapy (AI). For more detailed guidance, refer to the Perinatal Treatment Guidelines. The Stanford University HIV Drug Resistance Database provides valuable resources for interpreting genotypic resistance test results. Various tools are now available to assist clinicians in interpreting these results. Clinical trials have demonstrated that consulting with specialists in HIV drug resistance improves virologic outcomes. Clinicians are therefore encouraged to seek specialist consultation to interpret genotypic test results and design an optimal new regimen. Phenotypic assays measure the ability of a virus to replicate in the presence of varying concentrations of ARV drugs. These assays involve inserting patient-derived HIV gene sequences (e.g., reverse transcriptase, protease, integrase, or envelope genes) into a laboratory clone of HIV or generating pseudotyped viruses expressing the patient-derived genes of interest. Viral replication at different drug concentrations is monitored using a reporter gene and compared to a reference HIV strain. Automated phenotypic assays, which can produce results in 2–3 weeks, are commercially available but are more expensive than genotypic assays. Phenotypic assays provide fold resistance values (e.g., fold increase in IC50) associated with drug failure, though clinically significant fold resistance cutoffs are available for only some drugs. Consultation with a specialist to interpret test results is recommended. Limitations of both genotypic and phenotypic assays include the lack of uniform quality assurance for all available tests, high costs, and insensitivity to minor viral species. Drug-resistant viruses constituting less than 10–20% of the circulating viral population are unlikely to be detected by commercially available assays. When selective pressure from ARV drugs is removed, wild-type virus often re-emerges as the predominant population in plasma, reducing the proportion of resistant virus below the 10–20% detection threshold. For some drugs, this reversion to wild-type virus can occur within 4–6 weeks after discontinuation. However, clinical studies have shown that re-initiation of the same ARV agents (or those with similar resistance pathways) is usually associated with early drug failure, as the virus present at failure is derived from previously archived resistant virus. Resistance testing is most valuable when performed before or within four weeks of discontinuing ARV drugs (AII). In some patients, resistant virus may persist in plasma for longer periods, and resistance testing conducted 4–6 weeks after drug discontinuation may still detect mutations. However, the absence of detectable resistance in such cases must be interpreted cautiously when designing subsequent ARV regimens. The use of resistance assays in clinical practice is critical for determining initial treatment. Transmission of drug-resistant HIV strains is well-documented and associated with suboptimal virologic response to initial ART. The likelihood of acquiring drug-resistant virus depends on the prevalence of drug resistance in HIV-infected individuals engaging in high-risk behaviors within the community. In the United States and Europe, recent studies estimate that 6–16% of transmitted viruses are resistant to at least one ARV drug, with up to 8% (but generally less than 5%) exhibiting resistance to drugs from more than one class. If therapy is initiated in a person with early HIV infection, baseline resistance testing can guide regimen selection to optimize virologic response, making resistance testing in this context strongly recommended (AII). A genotypic assay is preferred for this purpose (AIII). In this setting, treatment initiation should not be delayed while awaiting resistance testing results. Once results are available, the treatment regimen can be modified if necessary. In the absence of therapy, resistant viruses may decline over time to levels below the detection limit of standard resistance tests. However, when therapy is eventually initiated, even low-level resistant viruses may increase the risk of treatment failure. Therefore, if therapy is deferred, resistance testing should still be performed during acute HIV infection (AIII). In such cases, the genotypic resistance test result may be kept on record until the patient is ready to start ART.
